data.study_type: simulation study with reinforcement learning agents
data.setting: Enhanced Reconfigurable Manufacturing System (EnhancedRMS) environment, a flexible job shop with 5 machines, 50 jobs, dynamic setup operations and stochastic machine breakdowns
data.sample_or_dataset: 50 jobs per episode, 1000 episodes per configuration; 5 independent runs per workload; 5 scheduling strategies compared
data.ai_method: Dueling-Attention Deep Q-Network (EnhancedDQN) with negotiation-driven coordination (deep reinforcement learning with multi‑agent negotiation)
data.comparison: PPO, SAC, EDF heuristic, Random baseline, and configurations with/without reconfiguration and negotiation (WNR, WTR, WNF, WTF)
data.key_findings: The negotiation‑driven EnhancedDQN achieved the lowest makespan (average 177.3 time units across configurations) and lowest total tardiness (average 312.7 time units) compared to other strategies. It also maintained high machine utilization (average 21.1%) while incurring moderate reconfiguration overhead (average 108.2 time units). In breakdown scenarios, the combined approach reduced makespan by 15.5% relative to reconfiguration‑only and improved utilization by 9.3 percentage points, achieving 100% job completion.
data.limitations: Results are based on a custom simulation environment; real‑world validation is lacking. The study reports variability due to stochastic disruptions but does not explore scalability to larger systems or multiple resource types. Computational efficiency and integration with existing manufacturing execution systems were not evaluated.
data.title: A Negotiation-Based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Approach for Dynamic Scheduling of Reconfigurable Manufacturing Systems

data.justification: The study clearly states its aim to evaluate a negotiation‑based MARL approach for dynamic scheduling in reconfigurable manufacturing systems. The experimental design is appropriate: a custom simulation environment (EnhancedRMS) with realistic job and machine parameters, multiple scenarios (normal vs. breakdown), and comparison against several baseline algorithms. Sample size is adequate—1000 episodes per configuration and five independent runs—providing statistical consistency. Outcome measures (makespan, utilization, tardiness, setup time, reconfigurations) are valid, well‑defined, and reported with means and standard deviations. Limitations are acknowledged (e.g., variability due to stochastic disruptions, need for more realistic industrial data, lack of real‑world deployment). However, the study remains a simulation‑based evaluation; external validity to actual manufacturing plants is not established, which tempers the overall confidence. Hence a moderate rating is appropriate.

data.setting: semiconductor manufacturing capacity planning using discrete-event simulation
data.sample_or_dataset: Intel’s small-scale Minifab (5 machines, 3 products) and SMT2020 testbed (1,314 machines, 583 processing steps, LV/HM dataset)
data.ai_method: deep reinforcement learning with a heterogeneous graph neural network (HGNN) trained via PPO
data.comparison: heuristic baseline, random actions, and no-action baseline
data.key_findings: In the Minifab environment, the HGNN policy increased completed lots by 1.59% and reduced cycle time by 2.70% versus the heuristic, and by 13.85%/14.96% versus no action. In the larger SMT2020 testbed, the policy improved completed lots by 1.87% (≈110 lots) and reduced cycle time by 1.80% (≈1.08 days) versus the heuristic, and by 2.50%/2.33% versus no action, yielding an overall throughput increase of about 1.8%.
data.limitations: Results are based on simulation testbeds; real‑world deployment and cost considerations were not evaluated; training stability over long horizons remains to be addressed.
data.title: Learning to Optimize Capacity Planning in Semiconductor Manufacturing

data.justification: The study clearly states its aim to evaluate a DRL‑based capacity planning policy, uses a suitable simulation‑based experimental design with two testbeds (Minifab and SMT2020), and reports quantitative performance metrics (completed lots, cycle time, daily going rate). However, the paper does not explicitly discuss how limitations (e.g., simulation fidelity, generalizability to real factories, or potential biases) are addressed, leaving that criterion unclear. Overall, the evidence supports a moderate quality rating.

data.study_type: simulation study using high‑fidelity digital twin
data.sample_or_dataset: high‑fidelity simulator based on real industrial data; 30 scenario–seed evaluation instances from 10 test scenarios and 3 seeds each
data.ai_method: deep reinforcement learning with event‑driven temporal‑difference formulation; algorithms evaluated include DQL, SAC, PPO, CQL, IQL
data.comparison: random policy, shortest processing time (SPT) heuristic, first‑in‑first‑out (FIFO) baseline
data.key_findings: Agents trained offline and online achieved significant and consistent gains in throughput and utilization compared to random, SPT, and FIFO baselines. Offline training with conservative algorithms (CQL, IQL) produced performance close to DQL, while online off‑policy methods (DQL, SAC) were more sample‑efficient and on‑policy PPO was more sensitive to data. Overall, the event‑driven RL framework enabled scalable, generalizable control in a large‑scale, stochastic semiconductor fab.
data.limitations: State and action representations were feature‑based; learned encoders, graph‑based or foundation‑model representations were not explored. Hyperparameter tuning and benchmarking across algorithms were limited; model‑based agents and self‑supervised dynamics learning were suggested for future work.
data.title: Event-Driven Reinforcement Learning Enables Long-Horizon Control in Semiconductor Fabrication

data.justification: The study clearly states its objective to optimize production control in semiconductor fabrication using deep reinforcement learning and evaluates performance through throughput and utilization metrics across 30 scenario–seed simulation instances. The design is appropriate, employing a centralized event‑driven framework with multiple RL algorithms and a rigorous evaluation protocol. Data adequacy is supported by high‑fidelity simulations derived from real industrial data. Outcome measures are valid and directly linked to production KPIs. The authors acknowledge limitations (feature‑based representations, lack of real‑world deployment) and outline future work. However, the evidence is limited to simulation, so while the methodology is sound, external validity remains uncertain, warranting a moderate overall rating.
